problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=3{e}^{2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+Bx{e}^{2x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.

activity_context.topic_title: Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODEs With Exponential Forcing

examples.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}^2 y}{\textrm{d} x^2} - 6\frac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d} x} + 9y = e ^{3x}.
$$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the complementary solution by solving the associated homogeneous ODE. Since the characteristic equation has a single repeated root $\lambda = 3,$ the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^{3x} + Bxe^{3x}.
$$

Second, we find a particular solution of the inhomogeneous ODE. We see that the right-hand side is $e^{3x},$ and $e^{3x}$ and $xe^{3x}$ are both terms in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x^2e ^ {3x},
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of $y_p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $y_p$, $y'_p$ and $y_p''$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(9{x}^{2}+12x+2)\alpha {e}^{3x}-6(3{x}^{2}+2x)\alpha {e}^{3x}+9\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ (9{x}^{2}+12x+2-18{x}^{2}-12x+9{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ 2\alpha  & =1 \\ \alpha  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
y_p(x) = \dfrac 1 2x^2 e ^{3x},
$$

and the general solution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={y}_{c}+{y}_{p} \\  & =A{e}^{3x}+Bx{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=6{e}^{3x}.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-5\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =2$ or $\lambda =3$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{3x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p}$, ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}-5(\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x})+6(\alpha x{e}^{3x}) & =6{e}^{3x} \\ (9x+6-5-15x+6x)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =6{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha {e}^{3x} & =6{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=6x{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{3x}+6x{e}^{3x}.
$$
